period_summary: The vast majority of patristic citations cluster in the 3rd and 4th centuries CE, driven almost entirely by the Arian controversy: both sides claimed Proverbs 8:22 as a proof-text, generating an unusually dense and textually self-conscious body of exegesis that reveals competing text forms in active circulation simultaneously.

citations.cited_text: Κύριος ἔκτισέν με ἀρχὴν ὁδῶν αὐτοῦ εἰς ἔργα αὐτοῦ
citations.text_form_note: Origen's citation follows the LXX closely with ἔκτισέν ('created'), the key verb of the Greek tradition, and the prepositional phrase εἰς ἔργα αὐτοῦ matches the Göttingen LXX apparatus for Proverbs 8:22. His Hexaplaric activity means he was acutely aware of the Hebrew ‎קָנָנִי (qānānî, 'acquired/possessed'), yet he still operates primarily from the LXX text form in non-Hexaplaric contexts.
citations.theological_use: Origen applies the verse to the generation of the Son from the Father before all creation, understanding 'created' in the LXX as referring to the Incarnate Wisdom rather than the eternal Logos, a distinction he introduces to preserve the Son's divine pre-existence. This nuanced reading would influence all subsequent Nicene and anti-Arian exegesis.
citations.transmission_implication: Origen's citation confirms that by the mid-3rd century, ἔκτισέν was the standard Greek text form known in Alexandria, even among scholars with Hebrew competence, establishing the LXX form as the dominant ecclesiastical text.

citations.work: Thalia (fragments preserved in Athanasius, De Synodis)
citations.cited_text: Κύριος ἔκτισέν με ἀρχὴν ὁδῶν αὐτοῦ
citations.text_form_note: Arius's use of ἔκτισέν is unambiguous and central to his entire theological system; the LXX's 'created' is precisely the reading upon which his Christology depends, and there is no indication from Athanasius's polemical reporting that Arius ever acknowledged an alternative reading. The citation is a truncated form of the LXX text but preserves the key lexeme unchanged.
citations.theological_use: Arius employs this verse as his primary scriptural proof that the Son is a creature (κτίσμα), arguing that 'the Lord created me' establishes the Son's ontological subordination to and temporal origin from the Father, making him the 'first of created things' rather than co-eternal God.
citations.transmission_implication: The Arian deployment of ἔκτισέν confirms that no alternative Greek reading (e.g., ἐκτήσατο) was yet widely known in Alexandrian circles, since Arius would otherwise have had to engage with a rival text form.

citations.cited_text: Κύριος ἔκτισέν με ἀρχὴν ὁδῶν αὐτοῦ εἰς ἔργα αὐτοῦ
citations.text_form_note: Athanasius cites the LXX form repeatedly and extensively across multiple chapters of Orationes II, always with ἔκτισέν; his entire anti-Arian exegetical strategy is to reinterpret this verb rather than to contest the Greek text itself, which he accepts as authoritative. He never appeals to the Hebrew qānānî or to Aquila's ἐκτήσατο as a correction of the LXX.
citations.theological_use: Athanasius accepts ἔκτισέν as the canonical text but argues extensively that 'created' here refers to the humanity of the Incarnate Son (or to his role as mediator of creation), not to the eternal Son's ontological origin, thereby defending Nicene co-equality without emending the text.
citations.transmission_implication: Athanasius's refusal to escape the exegetical problem by appealing to the Hebrew or to Aquila reveals that the LXX form ἔκτισέν was so entrenched as the ecclesiastical text in Greek-speaking Christianity that even the greatest Nicene polemicist had to argue within it rather than around it.

citations.chapter_section: Eccl. Theol. III.2; Dem. Ev. V.1
citations.cited_text: Κύριος ἔκτισέν με ἀρχὴν ὁδῶν αὐτοῦ
citations.text_form_note: Eusebius, trained in Origen's Hexaplaric library at Caesarea, cites the LXX form ἔκτισέν but in several contexts acknowledges the Hebrew and Aquila's ἐκτήσατο ('possessed/acquired'), making his overall usage 'mixed' in that he works between text forms even when citing the LXX as primary. In Eccl. Theol. III.2 he explicitly discusses the interpretive difference between the two verbs.
citations.theological_use: Eusebius uses the verse to support a subordinationist Christology broadly sympathetic to Arius but not identical to it, treating Wisdom as a real but secondary divine hypostasis whose 'creation' marks the beginning of the divine economy, and he uses the Hebrew/Aquila reading to argue for a richer semantic range than pure ontological subordination.
citations.transmission_implication: Eusebius is one of the earliest fathers to explicitly invoke the Hebrew tradition (via Aquila) alongside the LXX for this verse, suggesting that Hexaplaric scholarship at Caesarea created awareness of the textual plurality that would later be exploited by Nicene apologists.

citations.cited_text: Dominus condidit me initium viarum suarum in opera sua
citations.text_form_note: Hilary's Latin condidit ('founded/established') is a rendering of Greek ἔκτισέν rather than of Hebrew qānānî, and it tracks the Old Latin (Vetus Latina) tradition that derives from the Greek LXX rather than from any proto-MT tradition; it is categorically distinct from Aquila's possedit or Jerome's later Hebrew-based possedere. Hilary's text thus represents the Western reception of the Alexandrian LXX form.
citations.theological_use: Writing as a Latin Nicene bishop who had encountered Arianism in exile in the East, Hilary devotes an entire book (XII) of De Trinitate to refuting the Arian reading of this verse, arguing that condidit refers to the Son's assumption of human nature in the Incarnation, not to his eternal generation.
citations.transmission_implication: Hilary's Old Latin citation confirms that the LXX-derived text form (ἔκτισέν / condidit) had been transmitted into Latin Christianity via the Vetus Latina before any Hebraica veritas correction, demonstrating the LXX's reach into the Western text tradition.

citations.cited_text: Κύριος ἔκτισέν με ἀρχὴν ὁδῶν αὐτοῦ
citations.text_form_note: Basil cites the standard LXX text with ἔκτισέν without apparent awareness of or interest in alternative versions; unlike Eusebius he does not invoke Hexaplaric alternatives. His citation form is consistent across his correspondence and homilies where the verse is alluded to, suggesting a single stable LXX text form in his library.
citations.theological_use: Basil argues against Eunomius that ἔκτισέν in Proverbs 8:22 refers to the Son's role as beginning and first principle of God's works toward creation, not to an ontological act of creation of the Son himself, thereby defending the Nicene homoousion while accepting the LXX text.
citations.transmission_implication: Basil's citation shows that the post-Hexaplaric generation in Cappadocia continued to use the LXX form as normative without feeling compelled to engage the Hebrew alternative, suggesting that the Hexaplaric column had not displaced the LXX as the working ecclesiastical text.

citations.work: Epistulae / Commentarii in Proverbia (fragmentary) / Adversus Helvidium and related
citations.chapter_section: Ep. 140; Brev. in Ps. references; Commentarioli
citations.cited_text: Dominus possedit me in initio viarum suarum, antequam quicquam faceret a principio
citations.text_form_note: Jerome's Vulgate and his own citations consistently render Hebrew qānānî as possedit ('possessed/acquired'), following the MT tradition and the Hebrew witnesses he worked with in Bethlehem, in conscious departure from the LXX ἔκτισέν / condidit tradition. His addition of antequam quicquam faceret reflects the fuller MT verse structure (cf. MT 8:22–23) and agrees with Aquila and Symmachus rather than the LXX. This is a decisive closer_to_mt attestation in Latin Christianity.
citations.theological_use: Jerome uses possedit not primarily for Christological argumentation but to demonstrate the priority of the Hebrew text over the LXX and to provide Western Christians with a more accurate rendering; he is aware that possedit is less amenable to Arian interpretation than condidit/ἔκτισέν, though he does not exploit this polemically in most contexts.
citations.transmission_implication: Jerome's MT-aligned citation represents a pivotal moment in the Western transmission history, introducing a competing text form (possedit) that challenged the centuries-old Vetus Latina (condidit) and opened a new front in the textual history of the passage in Latin Christianity.

citations.work: Thesaurus de Sancta et Consubstantiali Trinitate
citations.cited_text: Κύριος ἔκτισέν με ἀρχὴν ὁδῶν αὐτοῦ εἰς ἔργα αὐτοῦ
citations.text_form_note: Cyril's citation in the Thesaurus follows the full LXX form including the prepositional phrase εἰς ἔργα αὐτοῦ, consistent with the Göttingen LXX Proverbs text. Writing in the 5th century, Cyril still shows no sign of adopting the Hebrew-based ἐκτήσατο reading, confirming that the LXX remained the operative text in Alexandrian theology even after Jerome's Hebraica veritas campaign.
citations.theological_use: Cyril deploys the verse as a Christological locus in the Thesaurus, following Athanasius's interpretive strategy of applying 'created' to the humanity of Christ rather than to the eternal Logos, and uses it within his broader argument for the Son's consubstantiality (ὁμοούσιον) with the Father.
citations.transmission_implication: Cyril's 5th-century LXX citation at Alexandria, unaffected by Jerome's MT-based revision, demonstrates the enduring independence and authority of the Greek LXX tradition in the Eastern church even when a Hebraically corrected alternative was available.

transmission_synthesis: The patristic citation history of Proverbs 8:22 is dominated by the LXX form ἔκτισέν ('created'), which was universally operative in Greek-speaking Christianity from Origen through Cyril of Alexandria and in Latin Christianity (as condidit) via the Vetus Latina, while the MT tradition's qānānî ('acquired/possessed') remained essentially invisible in ecclesiastical usage until Eusebius engaged it indirectly through Aquila and until Jerome introduced possedit into the Latin West via his Hebraica veritas project. The astonishing theological productivity of the Arian controversy paradoxically locked in the LXX text form as the authoritative reference point for both sides: neither Arius nor Athanasius found it strategically advantageous to appeal to the Hebrew, and this mutual acceptance of ἔκτισέν as the canonical text entrenched the LXX form deeply in the tradition. Eusebius of Caesarea represents a transitional moment in which Hexaplaric scholarship made the Hebrew reading available but not yet authoritative for theological argument, a liminal position that would not be resolved until Jerome's Latin translation. Collectively, the citations reveal that Proverbs 8:22 was transmitted in substantially stable LXX form across multiple regions (Alexandria, Caesarea, Asia Minor, the Latin West) without significant inner-Greek variation, implying a relatively uniform LXX Vorlage for Proverbs 8 in the 3rd–4th centuries, while the MT-aligned reading entered Western Christian consciousness as a late and deliberate scholarly intervention rather than a competing early tradition.
transmission_synthesis_plain: Almost all early Christian writers, whether arguing for or against Arius, used the same Greek translation which said God 'created' Wisdom, because that is what the standard Greek Bible (the LXX/Septuagint) said. The Hebrew original, which says God 'acquired' or 'possessed' Wisdom, was largely unknown to most Christians until Jerome translated the Bible into Latin directly from Hebrew in the late 4th century, introducing the word 'possessed' into Western Bibles. This means the theological battle over what Proverbs 8:22 meant was fought almost entirely on the terrain of the Greek translation rather than the Hebrew original.

notable_variants.significance: This is the most consequential single lexical variant in all of patristic exegesis: the LXX's choice of ἔκτισέν over a verb of acquisition or possession directly generated the Arian controversy, making this variant a case where a translation decision reshaped the entire Christological development of the 4th century.

The Old Latin rendering condidit confirms that the LXX's ἔκτισέν was transmitted into Latin Christianity via the Vetus Latina prior to Jerome, and its semantic range (slightly more 'founding/ordering' than 'creating from nothing') gave Latin Nicene theologians like Hilary a marginal exegetical advantage over those working in Greek.

Jerome's possedit, following the Hebrew qānānî via Aquila and Symmachus, introduced into Western Christianity a reading that fundamentally changes the meaning of the verse from a statement about creation to one of eternal possession, thereby removing the primary textual basis for Arian exegesis in Latin, though its impact on the Christological debate was felt only after the controversy's peak.

Aquila's translation ἐκτήσατο, corresponding to the Hebrew qānānî and noted in the Hexapla, appears in Eusebius's discussion as an alternative but is never adopted by any mainstream patristic author as a replacement for ἔκτισέν, demonstrating that Hexaplaric awareness of the MT tradition did not translate into ecclesiastical text revision in the Greek East before the 5th century.

bibcrit_assessment.title: Arian Controversy Locked In Divergent LXX Reading
bibcrit_assessment.reasoning: The most striking implication of this patristic citation history is that a single translational choice in the LXX — ἔκτισέν for Hebrew qānānî — became so embedded through the Arian controversy's mutual acceptance by both sides that the MT-aligned tradition (qānānî / possedit) had essentially no chance of displacing it in Greek Christianity, and entered Latin Christianity only through Jerome's deliberate scholarly act. This means the LXX's divergence from the MT at Proverbs 8:22 was not merely a textual curiosity but became institutionalized through centuries of intense theological controversy in which neither party had an incentive to correct the Greek text toward the Hebrew. The patristic evidence thus supports Hengel's thesis that the LXX functioned as an autonomous scriptural authority in the early church rather than as a subordinate translation of the Hebrew.
bibcrit_assessment.plain: The fact that both sides in the great 4th-century debate about Christ's nature used the same Greek translation — without either side pointing to the Hebrew original as a corrective — shows how deeply the Septuagint had become the Christian Bible, independent of the Hebrew text from which it was translated. Jerome's later effort to align Latin Bibles with Hebrew was a minority scholarly position that arrived too late to change the terms of the debate.

_validation.confidence_note: The analysis captures the broad and well-known contours of Proverbs 8:22's patristic reception accurately, but several specific citation references and attributions are imprecise, possibly fabricated, or overstated.

flagged_claims.claim: Origen of Alexandria, De Principiis I.2.1–3
flagged_claims.reason: While Origen does discuss Prov 8:22 in De Principiis I.2 (on Christ as Wisdom), the precise citation of the Greek text in this section comes through Rufinus's Latin translation; the reconstructed Greek wording attributed here may not be directly verifiable from De Principiis itself.

flagged_claims.claim: Athanasius, Orationes contra Arianos Or. II.18–82 (esp. II.44–46)
flagged_claims.reason: Athanasius's extended treatment of Prov 8:22 is in Oration II, but the specific subdivision 'II.18–82' is unusually wide and the focal sections 'II.44–46' should be verified; standard reference is to Or. II.44ff. but the range cited needs checking.

flagged_claims.claim: Eusebius, Eccl. Theol. III.2; Dem. Ev. V.1
flagged_claims.reason: Eusebius does discuss Prov 8:22 in Demonstratio Evangelica V, but the specific chapter references and the claim that he 'explicitly discusses the interpretive difference between the two verbs' in Eccl. Theol. III.2 needs verification; this could be a confident-sounding but imprecise citation.

The reference 'Thes. Ass. 18' is not a standard citation format for Cyril's Thesaurus de Sancta Trinitate, which is normally cited by 'assertio' or chapter number. The notation appears garbled or invented; while Cyril does treat Prov 8:22 in the Thesaurus, the precise locus given is unreliable.

flagged_claims.claim: Jerome, Ep. 140; Brev. in Ps. references; Commentarioli
flagged_claims.reason: Epistula 140 is on Psalm 90 and does not have Prov 8:22 as a focus; Jerome did not write a surviving full commentary on Proverbs (the 'Commentarii in Proverbia' is largely fragmentary or spurious). The bundling of references here is vague and partially misleading.

flagged_claims.claim: Arius's cited text from Thalia preserved in De Synodis 15
flagged_claims.reason: While Athanasius's De Synodis 15 does preserve Thalia fragments, attributing a specific citation form of Prov 8:22 to Arius's own words (rather than to Athanasius's polemical paraphrase) is more confident than the evidence permits.

flagged_claims.claim: Hilary, De Trinitate XII.35–48 devotes 'an entire book (XII)' to refuting the Arian reading of this verse
flagged_claims.reason: Hilary does treat Prov 8:22 in De Trinitate XII, but the claim that the 'entire book' is devoted to this verse overstates the case; book XII addresses Wisdom Christology more broadly.

Basil discusses Prov 8:22 in Adversus Eunomium, but the principal locus is generally cited around II.20 or later; precise section needs verification, and the claim that Basil shows no awareness of Hexaplaric alternatives may be overstated given his Cappadocian context.

flagged_claims.claim: Eusebius is one of the earliest fathers to explicitly invoke the Hebrew tradition (via Aquila) alongside the LXX for this verse
flagged_claims.reason: This historiographical claim about Eusebius's priority requires verification; Origen himself, via the Hexapla, would have engaged Aquila's reading earlier, which the analysis itself implies.

safe_claims: The LXX uses ἔκτισέν while the MT uses קָנָנִי (qānānî)
Aquila renders the Hebrew with ἐκτήσατο
Both Arian and Nicene parties used Prov 8:22 as a proof-text
Athanasius accepted ἔκτισέν and reinterpreted it Christologically rather than emending the text
Jerome's Vulgate renders the verse with possedit, aligning with the MT tradition
The Vetus Latina tradition rendered the verse with condidit, derived from the Greek LXX
Patristic engagement with this verse intensified during the 3rd–4th century Arian controversy
